title: Water a house plant at its roots without wetting its leaves
instruction: Water the plant at its roots, onto the soil, without wetting its leaves. Then put the jug back on its stool, leave the plant's leaves as they were and take both arms back to where they started.
context: Many house plants (and seedlings, and vegetables in a bed) must be watered at the soil, not over the leaves, which rot or scorch when wet; with leaves spread over the pot, one hand holds the foliage aside while the other pours, as in caring for plants at home, in a nursery or in a care home.
setup: A table in front of two arms (bases 61 cm apart), seen by one overhead camera and a camera on each wrist. Distances are measured forward from the line between the arm bases and sideways from the midpoint between them. (1) A terracotta pot 17 cm across and 7.5 cm tall on a saucer, its middle 30 cm forward and 2 cm right of the centre line, filled with dark soil 1.3 cm below its rim; fixed. In it a house plant with a green stem and broad leaves (15 cm long, up to 13 cm wide) spread low over the soil: three fixed in the crown, over the back and both sides of the pot, and one big leaf in front on a springy stalk, joined to the stem 10 cm above the table, lying over the front of the soil and reaching out 6 cm past the rim toward the arms. Pushed round on its stalk, the big leaf springs back over the soil when let go. (2) A blue plastic watering jug (5.4 cm across, 8.5 cm tall, with a pouring lip and a handle) holding 120 ml of water, simulated as 12 drops (7 mm beads, 10 ml each), standing on a beech stool 6 cm tall, 26 cm forward and 13 cm left of the centre line. The layout is the same in every trial, as in the screenshot. Real trial: an ordinary artificial house plant (an artificial peace lily, say) with moulded green plastic leaves, which take up no water, 15 cm long and up to 13 cm wide, set as above: three in the crown over the back and sides of the pot, and the big lower leaf on a sprung wire stalk lying over the front of the soil, which springs back when let go. Each leaf is fixed to its wire stalk with a small clip, so it can be unclipped for the weighings. The plant stands in real potting soil, just moist, in the same 17 cm glazed terracotta pot on its saucer, with the drainage hole plugged by a rubber bung for the trial. The jug (about 150 ml) holds 120 ml of room-temperature water tinted dark blue with food colouring, so water on a green leaf shows clearly. Two cameras film the trial at 60 frames a second, synchronized: one overhead and one from the side, level with the leaves.
scoring: Judged at the end. Real trial (1 g of water = 1 ml): (a) water delivered to the soil: the pot is weighed in the same state before and after, with its four plastic leaves unclipped (it keeps its soil, stem, wire stalks, clips and bung). Before the trial, unclip the leaves, lift the pot out of its saucer and weigh it, and the dry saucer, on a kitchen scale (1 g steps), then clip the leaves back on; after the trial, photograph the leaves (below), unclip them, lift the pot out, let it drip into the saucer, and weigh the pot and the saucer. The pot's gain is the water delivered to the soil (its drainage hole is plugged, and the 1.3 cm of headroom above the soil holds about 235 ml, so none leaves the pot); the saucer's gain is spilled water and never counts as delivered. (b) leaf contact is observed, not measured: the two synchronized 60 fps videos (overhead, and from the side level with the leaves) are reviewed frame by frame, and any frame in which the stream or a droplet of the blue water touches a leaf counts as leaf contact. As a backup, every leaf is photographed close up after the trial, before it is unclipped; a blue droplet or wet mark on it also counts as contact. The leaves are plastic and nothing is weighed on them, so the result does not depend on how much water a leaf holds or whether it runs off. Any leaf contact scores 0.0, as it breaks the instruction's constraint. Simulation: each of the 12 beads stands for 10 ml. A bead counts as leaf contact if it ever comes within 4 mm of any leaf, checked after every physics step (240 times a second); it counts as delivered only if it ends lying on the soil inside the pot's wall (its centre within 7.25 cm of the pot's axis and between 3 mm below and 15 mm above the soil's surface) without ever having touched a leaf. Beads that miss the pot, bounce out of it or land in the saucer never count. 0.0 if any bead ever touched a leaf (any leaf contact in a real trial). Otherwise 1.0: at least 90 ml delivered (pot gain at least 90 g; 9 beads), the jug back on its stool (within 3 cm, upright within 15 degrees), the big leaf back over the soil (within 12 degrees of where it lay), both hands let go (each TCP at least 4 cm from the jug and the leaf) and both arms back where they started (each TCP within 5 cm); in a real trial the end state is checked against marks on the stool and the pot's rim (ruler and protractor) and the robot's joint log. 0.5: at least 90 ml delivered (pot gain at least 90 g; 9 beads), without the end state. 0.25: at least 40 ml delivered (pot gain at least 40 g; 4 beads). Else 0.0. The trial ends at the run limit, or once the full score has held for 1 s with the jug, the big leaf and every bead still.
reset_notes: Pull the bung and let the pot drain, then plug it again (it is weighed afresh, leaves unclipped, before each trial); empty and dry the saucer; wipe the plastic leaves dry and clip them back on; lay the big leaf back over the soil; refill the jug with 120 ml of the tinted water and stand it on its stool.
fidelity: Rigid-body PhysX (Isaac Sim 6.1, 240 Hz physics, 20 Hz control). Simplified: the 120 ml of water is 12 rigid 7 mm beads (10 ml each, 0.8 g) that do not cling or splash; a bead within 4 mm of a leaf counts as touching it (a real trial judges contact from 60 fps video). The saucer is drawn only. Leaves are rigid plates (plastic in a real trial); the crown's leaves and the pot are fixed, and the big leaf turns on its stalk against a spring (0.0016 N m per degree).
